real_s1.explanation: The unit responds to a large, close-up dog face that looks toward the camera and is not blocked by anything. It is driven by how big and how frontal the face is, not by fur color.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds to a large, close-up dog face that looks toward the camera and is not blocked by anything. It is driven by how big and how frontal the face is, not by fur color.
parsed.evidence: Head size in the frame held strongly (d +1.72, percentile 100) and a clear, camera-facing face also held (d +1.07, percentile 98). The light-versus-dark fur prediction failed (d +0.25, percentile 81), and one dog versus several came close but fell short (d +0.60, percentile 94).
parsed.missing_data: Controlled comparisons of frontal versus profile faces at the same head size would help, to see whether the two held effects are separate. Close-up faces of other animals, such as cats and wolves, would show whether the unit is specific to dogs.

real_s2.explanation: The unit responds to a single dog's face seen large, close-up and frontally, with both eyes and the nose clearly visible. Fur color does not appear to matter.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds to a single dog's face seen large, close-up and frontally, with both eyes and the nose clearly visible. Fur color does not appear to matter.
parsed.evidence: Head size (d +1.45, 99th percentile) and a fully visible face (d +1.09, 98th percentile) both held. Light versus dark face fur had almost no effect (d +0.13, 71st percentile), and one dog versus several fell just short (d +0.60, 94th percentile, with only 13 multi-dog photos).
parsed.missing_data: Close-up frontal faces of non-dog animals such as cats, foxes or bears, which would show whether the unit is specific to dogs, plus more photos with several dogs to settle the dog-count effect.

real_s3.explanation: The unit responds to a close-up, frontal portrait of a dog's face: a dog head that fills a large part of the frame and looks toward the camera. Fur color does not appear to matter.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds to a close-up, frontal portrait of a dog's face: a dog head that fills a large part of the frame and looks toward the camera. Fur color does not appear to matter.
parsed.evidence: Head size (d +1.45, 99th percentile) and facing the camera (d +1.11, 98th percentile) both held strongly, while light versus dark face color showed essentially no effect (d +0.06, 59th percentile). Single versus multiple dogs was positive but just missed the threshold (d +0.60, 94th percentile), which fits a preference for one large face rather than a separate number effect.
parsed.missing_data: Photos of close-up frontal faces of non-dog animals such as cats and wolves, or of humans, would show whether the unit is specific to dogs or responds to any large frontal face. Head-size results controlled for whether the face points at the camera would separate those two effects.

parsed.explanation: The unit appears to respond to dogs in general. Within dog classes it does not prefer close-up, light-furred, frontal single-dog portraits, and if anything it leans toward photos where the dog's head is small, such as whole-body or more distant views.
parsed.evidence: None of the four predictions held (percentiles 6–43). The head-size prediction reversed, with d -0.47 at the 6th percentile, so the unit is more active when the dog's head takes up less of the frame. Number of dogs, face color and face orientation showed essentially no effect.
parsed.missing_data: Direct tests of whole-body versus head-only framing and of dog size in the frame, plus the identities of the top classes, to confirm that dogs as a category are what drives the unit.
